retrieved.text: There are many ways of approaching this. Here is one. Let’s assume there are two groups of consumers: a low WTP group, e.g. students using your LLM to cheat on assignments, and a high WTP group, e.g. consulting firms using it to answer their clients’ questions. First, create a “base” and “premium” LLM. The premium could be more powerful, allow longer messages from the user, and so on. Next, choose the price - likely a subscription fee - for the base LLM that equals the students’ WTP. For the premium LLM, choose the price that makes the consulting firms indifferent between buying the base or premium version. This will induce each group to reveal themselves through self-selection. Note that whether this yields more profit than simple pricing depends on the groups’ WTP relative to marginal cost, so you should use A/B tests to see whether this or simple pricing yields more profit.

Theoretically, both producer and consumer surplus could rise with scalable price targeting.
Revenues relative to control pricing increase 65% with optimised uniform pricing, but 81.5% with scalable price targeting. This gives 10% higher profits with scalable price targeting vs optimised uniform pricing
Customer surplus declines by less than 1% with price targeting, but 70% of customers pay less than the uniform price.
Generally negative views of differential pricing fuelled by big data – CEA (2015) finds differential pricing transfers value from consumers to shareholders, which increases inequality and inefficiency.

Recent debates highlighted how U.S. patients often pay more for identical medicines than patients abroad. For example, while Americans paid an average price of $2,700 for Humira, the Swiss were able to buy the same drug for $800, and in the United Kingdom, patients got it for $1,300. This disparity has drawn bipartisan criticism, leading to recent policy pushes — including proposals to tie U.S. prices to the lowest prices in peer nations — aimed at narrowing the gap.
Why this is third-degree price discrimination:
Heterogeneity in willingness to pay: U.S. patients and insurers have historically accepted higher prices due to higher incomes and insurance coverage.
Ability to identify groups: Geography provides a clear and enforceable distinction. U.S. sales are tracked through the FDA and domestic distribution, while foreign sales move through national health systems.
